::: {.key-question}
What chronic health conditions are experienced by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples in the NEPHU catchment?
:::

**Key points from stakeholder consultation**

- At stakeholder consultation during the development of this report, the discussion included reflections that Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people may be diagnosed with cancer at a later stage of disease or at a younger age than non-Indigenous people, which may impact on recorded cancer rates and survivability.

- Different types of cancers may also be more frequent among Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people compared to non-Indigenous people.

## Testing for Cancer

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Testing for cancer
# Data from ABS National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in NATSIHS data
testing_cancer_male <- f_read_natsihs_sex("Indicator_Vic_Sex_Cancer_TestMale.csv") %>% 
  dplyr::filter(sex == "Male")

testing_cancer_female <- f_read_natsihs_sex("Indicator_Vic_Sex_Cancer_TestFemale.csv") %>% 
  dplyr::filter(sex == "Female")

testing_cancer <- testing_cancer_male %>% 
  dplyr::bind_rows(testing_cancer_female) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(breast_n = dplyr::case_when(
    sex == "Male" ~ 0,
    TRUE ~ breast_n))

# Data wrangling
testing_cancer <- testing_cancer %>% 
  dplyr::rowwise() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(nottested_n = not_applicable_n,
                answered_n  = total_n) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  #
  janitor::adorn_totals(fill = "Total") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::rename(skin_n = skin_cancer_n,
                lung_n = lung_cancer_n,
                cervical_n = cervical_cancer_n) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(across(bowel_n:nottested_n,
                       ~ . / answered_n * 100,
                       .names = "{.col}_prop"),
                #
                answered_prop = answered_n / answered_n * 100) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::rename_with(~ stringr::str_replace(., "_n_prop$", "_prop"), ends_with("_n_prop"))

testing_cancer <- testing_cancer %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
    prostate_prop = dplyr::case_when(
      iare_name == "Total" ~ testing_cancer$prostate_prop[1],
      TRUE ~ prostate_prop),
    #
    cervical_prop = dplyr::case_when(
      iare_name == "Total" ~ testing_cancer$cervical_prop[2],
      TRUE ~ cervical_prop)) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::select(sex,
                starts_with("bowel"),
                starts_with("breast"),
                starts_with("cervical"),
                starts_with("lung"),
                starts_with("prostate"),
                starts_with("skin"),
                starts_with("other"),
                starts_with("nottested"),
                starts_with("answered")) %>% 
  #
  tidyr::pivot_longer(!sex,
                      names_to      = c("answer", ".value"),
                      names_pattern = "(.+)_(.+)") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(answer = factor(dplyr::recode(answer,
                                              "bowel"     = "Bowel cancer",
                                              "breast"    = "Breast cancer",
                                              "cervical"  = "Cervical cancer",
                                              "lung"      = "Lung cancer",
                                              "prostate"  = "Prostate cancer",
                                              "skin"      = "Skin cancer",
                                              "other"     = "Other cancers",
                                              "nottested" = "Never tested",
                                              "answered"  = "Total"),
                                levels = c("Bowel cancer",
                                           "Breast cancer",
                                           "Cervical cancer",
                                           "Lung cancer",
                                           "Prostate cancer",
                                           "Skin cancer",
                                           "Other cancers",
                                           "Never tested",
                                           "Total")))
```

- Data for this topic were obtained from the [2022-23 ABS National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/aboriginal-and-torres-strait-islander-peoples/national-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-islander-health-survey/latest-release).

- Overall, 35% of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander survey respondents living in Greater Melbourne reported that they had been tested for cancer, either for screening or diagnostic purposes. This equates to approximately 13,500 Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people.

- Prostate cancer (20%) and bowel cancer (13%) were the most common cancer types tested for among males.

- Cervical cancer (53%) and breast cancer (26%) were the most common cancer types tested for among females.

::: {.callout-tip title="Definitions and notes about this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- Data for this topic were collected from all people completing the 2022-23 ABS National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Survey.

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- `r note_aboriginality_natsihs`

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- People were classified as having been tested for cancer if they stated that they had ever been tested for any type of cancer, had ever been tested for prostate cancer by rectal examination, prostate specific antigen blood test, and/or transrectal ultrasound, ever had a mammogram, and/or ever had a Pap smear.
:::

## Cancer

### Self-Reported Cancer

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cancer, by LGA
# Data from ABS Census using TableBuilderPro
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in Census data
cancer_lga <- f_read_census_lga("Aboriginal_Health_Cancer_LGA.csv",
                                variable = "cancer") %>% 
  # 
  dplyr::filter(cancer != "Not stated")

# Data wrangling
cancer_lga <- cancer_lga %>%
  #
  dplyr::mutate(cancer = dplyr::case_when(
    cancer == "Has cancer (including remission)" ~ "yes",
    TRUE ~ "no")) %>% 
  #
  f_wrangle_census_lga(variable = cancer,
                       level    = "person",
                       dichot   = "yes")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cancer, by age and sex
# Data from ABS Census using TableBuilderPro
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in Census data
cancer_agesex <- f_read_census_agesex("Aboriginal_Health_Cancer_AgeSex.csv",
                                      variable = "cancer") %>% 
  #
  dplyr::filter(cancer != "Not stated")

# Data wrangling
cancer_agesex <- cancer_agesex %>% 
  #
  dplyr::mutate(cancer = dplyr::case_when(
    cancer == "Has cancer (including remission)" ~ "yes",
    TRUE ~ "no")) %>%  
  #
  f_wrangle_census_agesex(variable = cancer,
                          dichot   = "yes")
```

- Data for this topic were obtained from the [ABS Census 2021](https://www.abs.gov.au/census).

- Overall, 2.1% (n = 237) of people living in the NEPHU catchment who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander in the Census have been told by a doctor or nurse that they have cancer. This was lower than for non-Indigenous people living in the NEPHU catchment (2.8%), largely due to the younger age structure of the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander population.

- The number of people living in different LGAs within the NEPHU catchment who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander in the Census who have been told by a doctor or nurse that they have cancer ranged from 41 (Yarra Ranges LGA) to 5 (Nillumbik LGA).

- The percentage of people living in different LGAs within the NEPHU catchment who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander in the Census who have been told by a doctor or nurse that they have cancer ranged from 3.4% (Whitehorse LGA) to 1.3% (Darebin LGA).

- The number of people who have been told by a doctor or nurse that they have cancer was highest for people aged 50-59 or 60-69 years for both males and females, and the percentage of people who have been told by a doctor or nurse that they have cancer increased with increasing age.

- For people aged 50-69 years, the percentage of people who have been told by a doctor or nurse that they have cancer was higher for Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people than for non-Indigenous people, particularly for males aged 50-59 years.

::: {.callout-tip title="Definitions and notes about this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- Data for this topic were collected from all people completing the ABS Census 2021.

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- `r note_aboriginality_census`

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- People were classified as having cancer if they selected *Cancer (including remission)*.

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- Census respondents may have reported malignant and/or benign cancers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Census questions for this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- Has the person been told by a doctor or nurse that they have any of these long-term health conditions? (*Select all that apply*)
  - Arthritis
  - Asthma
  - Cancer (including remission)
  - Dementia (including Alzheimer's)  
  - Diabetes (excluding gestational diabetes)
  - Heart disease (including heart attack or angina)
  - Kidney disease
  - Lung condition (including COPD or emphysema)
  - Mental health condition (including depression or anxiety)
  - Stroke
  - Any other long-term health condition(s)
  - No long-term health condition

:::

### Top 10 Cancer Types

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Top 10 cancer types
# Data from Victorian Cancer Registry
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in Cancer Registry data
cancer_type <- readxl::read_excel(file.path(root_folder, subfolder_cancer, "Vic_Top10_Incidence_Deaths_Sex.xlsx"),
                                  skip  = 4,
                                  sheet = "VictoriaTop10Cases") %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>% 
  #
  dplyr::rename(aboriginal_n = n)
```

- Data for this indicator were obtained from the [Victorian Cancer Registry](https://www.cancervic.org.au/about-cancer/types/statistics).

- Between January 2018 and December 2022 the most common cancers diagnosed in people who identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander living in Victoria were lung cancer (n = 260), prostate cancer (n = 172), bowel cancer (n = 171), and breast cancer (n = 170).

- In comparison, during 2023 the most common cancer types diagnosed among all people living in Victoria were prostate cancer (n = 6,378), breast cancer (n = 5,197), bowel cancer (n = 3,779), and lung cancer (n = 3,435).

- Prostate cancer (n = 172) and lung cancer (n = 126) were the most common cancer types diagnosed among males.

- Breast cancer (n = 169) and lung cancer (n = 134) were the most common cancer types diagnosed among females.

::: {.callout-tip title="Definitions and notes about this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
- `r note_aboriginality_cancer`

<div style="height: 0.1em;"></div>

- Benign neoplasms and recurrent cancers were excluded from these data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="ICD-10-AM codes for this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
Cancer type is recorded in the Victorian Cancer Registry by converting [International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, 3rd Edition (ICD-O-3)](https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/other-classifications/international-classification-of-diseases-for-oncology) medical codes from patient records and cancer notifications to [International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems 10th Revision Australian Modification (ICD-10-AM)](https://www.ihacpa.gov.au/health-care/classification/icd-10-amachiacs) codes for malignant neoplasms.

The Top 10 cancer types presented in this report were from the following ICD-10-AM categories:

  - Lung: C33-C34
  - Prostate (male only): C61
  - Bowel: C18-C20
  - Breast (male and female): C50
  - Head and neck: C00-C14, C30-C32
  - Melanoma: C43
  - Primary liver: C22
  - Kidney: C64
  - Pancreas: C25
  - Uterine (female only): C54-C55

:::

### Hospital Admissions for Cancer

```{r}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Hospitalisations - cancer
# Data from PHIDU Social Health Atlas
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read in PHIDU data
hospital_cancer <- f_read_phidu_iare_hospital(data_sheet    = "Admissions_principal_diag",
                                              column_select = "admissions_for_cancer_aboriginal_people")

# Data wrangling
hospital_cancer <- hospital_cancer %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(iare_name = factor(iare_name, levels = iare_inc_vic_lvl)) %>% 
  #
  dplyr::arrange(iare_name)
```

- Data for this topic were obtained from the [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Health Atlas of Australia](https://phidu.torrens.edu.au/social-health-atlases), compiled from the [Victorian Admitted Episodes Dataset (VAED)](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/data-reporting/victorian-admitted-episodes-dataset).

- During the four-year period 01 July 2017 to 30 June 2021 there were 1,562 hospital admissions for cancer for Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people living in Greater Melbourne.

- The number of admissions for cancer for Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people living in different IAREs within the NEPHU catchment ranged from 207 (Northcote/Preston/Whittlesea IARE) to 28 (Maroondah IARE).

- The age-standardised rate of admissions for cancer for Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people living in different IAREs within the NEPHU catchment ranged from 1,418 per 100,000 population (Melbourne/Port Phillip IARE) to 767 per 100,000 population (Maroondah IARE).

- 5 of the 10 IAREs in the NEPHU catchment area had an age-standardised admission rate for cancer above the average rate for all Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people living in Greater Melbourne (Melbourne/Port Phillip, Yarra Ranges, Northcote/Preston/Whittlesea, Whitehorse, and Craigieburn/Sunbury IAREs).

::: {.callout-tip title="Definitions and notes about this topic" icon=false collapse=false}

::: {.callout-tip title="ICD-10-AM codes for this topic" icon=false collapse=false}
Admissions for cancer were defined as those with a principal diagnosis code in the following list, coded using the [International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems 10th Revision Australian Modification (ICD-10-AM)](https://www.ihacpa.gov.au/health-care/classification/icd-10-amachiacs):

  - C00-C97: Malignant neoplasms
  - D00-D09: *In-situ* neoplasms
  - D10-D36: Benign neoplasms
  - D37-D48: Neoplasms of uncertain or unknown behaviour

:::
